actions.body: The integration of AI-driven recommendations in sports training is often lauded for its scientific precision. However, recent cross-sectional data [source-d9addfec171d4b5d] highlights a concerning behavioral sequence. Athletes who become highly dependent on AI recommendations tend to outsource the monitoring of their own bodily signals. This 'body signal outsourcing' is linked to a reduced sense of self-regulation, as the athlete defers to the algorithm rather than their own internal physiological feedback. Consequently, this leads to hesitation when faced with training decisions not covered by the algorithm, ultimately eroding the athlete's training self-efficacy. These findings emphasize that while AI can provide efficiency, it may inadvertently atrophy the cognitive and regulatory processes essential for autonomous athletic judgment. Summary: The core issue identified is that algorithmic dependence in training may undermine an athlete's ability to interpret their own body and make independent decisions, turning tools of support into barriers to self-regulation.
actions.lede: New research suggests that relying on AI training recommendations may create a ripple effect that reduces an athlete's autonomy, leading to decreased self-efficacy.
actions.reason: Publishing summary of findings from the project on AI-driven training dependence and athlete autonomy.
actions.title: The Cost of Efficiency: AI Dependency in Athlete Decision-Making
